You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load ($R_L$ varies from 1M$\Omega$ to 10M$\Omega$) from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out, min} \ge 4.5$ V
        *   $V_{out, max} \le 5.5$ V
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (final window)
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02$ V
    *   Piezo model: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 M$\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.8$ V (at S1). This is *lower* than the target $V_{out}$ (4.5 V - 5.5 V), meaning we *must* use a step-up mechanism (like SSHI or a charge pump) or a transformer.

    *   `P-SSHI` (c0041):
        *   Topology: Full bridge rectifier (DSCH) + SSHI-like inductor switch ($L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel/series config).
        *   Score: 40.40.
        *   Passed: 2/6 (S2, S6).
        *   Failed:
            *   $V_{out, max} > 5.5$ V for S1, S3, S5.
            *   $V_{out, min} < 4.5$ V for S4.
            *   Settled $dv > 0.02$ V for S3, S5.
        *   S4 is the "weak excitation" case ($I_p = 40 \mu$A).
        *   S3 is the "strong excitation" case ($I_p = 120 \mu$A).
        *   S5 is "low frequency" ($f = 80$ Hz).
    *   `P-SSHI-Bleed` (c0042):
        *   Topology: Same as `P-SSHI` but with a bleed resistor $R_{bleed}$.
        *   Score: -13.98.
        *   Result: Total failure. Bleeding power is not the solution when $V_{out, min}$ is already failing on S4.

    *   The `P-SSHI` circuit is based on a Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) technique.
    *   It uses a full-bridge rectifier to convert the boosted piezo voltage to DC.
    *   The problem is the lack of voltage regulation. When the piezo is strong (S3), $V_{out}$ climbs too high. When the piezo is weak (S4), $V_{out}$ doesn't reach the threshold.
    *   We need a way to limit $V_{out}$ at 5.5 V without wasting too much energy, and we need to maximize efficiency to lift S4.

    *   The current `P-SSHI` topology uses a full bridge (4 diodes) and an inductor.
    *   To prevent $V_{out} > 5.5$ V, a Zener diode (DZ33) is available, but it's only 3.3 V. We need a 5.5 V limit.
    *   Wait, the components list says: `DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)`.
    *   If we put a DZ33 on the output, $V_{out}$ will be clamped to ~3.3 V, which is below $V_{out, min} = 4.5$ V. So a simple Zener clamp on the output won't work.

    *   *Wait*, can we use the Zener elsewhere? Or maybe a different regulator?
    *   We don't have an op-amp or a dedicated regulator chip. We only have R, L, C, D, S, SYNC.
    *   To limit $V_{out}$ to 5.5 V, we could try a shunt regulator made of diodes, but we don't have a 5.5 V zener.

    *   Let's look at the SSHI topology again. In P-SSHI, the inductor is used to flip the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   The current `P-SSHI` uses a full bridge. A full bridge has 2 diode drops ($\sim 0.5$ V total for DSCH).
    *   Maybe a half-bridge or a different rectification?

    *   The core problem for S4 is $V_{out, min}$.
    *   The core problem for S3 is $V_{out, max}$.
    *   S4: $I_p = 40 \mu$A, $R_L = 4.7$ M$\Omega$. Power needed $\approx 4.5^2 / 4.7\text{e}6 \approx 4.3 \mu$W.
    *   S3: $I_p = 120 \mu$A, $R_L = 10$ M$\Omega$. Power needed $\approx 4.5^2 / 10\text{e}6 \approx 2 \mu$W.

    *   How to limit $V_{out}$ without a 5.5 V Zener?
    *   Maybe a "crowbar" or a shunt? We can't build a precise 5.5 V shunt with only 3.3 V Zeners and diodes.
    *   Wait, if I put two DZ33 Zeners in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6$ V. Still not 5.5 V.
    *   What if I use a Zener in series with a diode? $3.3 + 0.25 = 3.55$ V.
    *   What if I use a Zener to control the switch? (No, the SYNC is ideal and based on piezo extrema).

    *   Let's rethink the SSHI. A standard SSHI uses a switch to invert the piezo voltage.
    *   `P-SSHI` (c0041) had:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn
    *   This looks like the inductor is in parallel with the piezo during the switch period.
    *   The full bridge rectifies the piezo voltage.

    *   *Correction on P-SSHI (c0041)*:
        pzp and pzn are the piezo terminals.
        L1 is connected from pzp to n1. S1 is connected from n1 to pzn.
        When S1 is closed, L1 is in parallel with the piezo (pzp to pzn).
        The bridge diodes (D1-D4) are also connected to pzp and pzn.
        This is a standard SSHI.

    *   Since the problem is mainly $V_{out, max}$ (too high) and $V_{out, min}$ (too low on S4), and we have no voltage regulator, we must rely on the storage capacitor $C_{out}$ and the load $R_L$.
    *   But $R_L$ is given. We can't change it.
    *   We can only change $C_{out}$ and the SSHI parameters.
    *   Wait, the `P-SSHI` score was 40.40. It almost passed!
    *   S1: $V_{avg}=5.57, V_{max}=5.58$ (Fail $V_{max} \le 5.5$ by 0.08 V)
    *   S2: $V_{avg}=5.08, V_{max}=5.1$ (Pass)
    *   S3: $V_{avg}=12.2, V_{max}=12.2$ (Fail $V_{max} \le 5.5$ by 6.7 V)
    *   S4: $V_{avg}=3.77, V_{max}=3.77$ (Fail $V_{min} \ge 4.5$ by 0.73 V)
    *   S5: $V_{avg}=6.09, V_{max}=6.1$ (Fail $V_{max} \le 5.5$ by 0.6 V)
    *   S6: $V_{avg}=4.71, V_{max}=4.72$ (Pass)

    *   The $V_{out}$ is too high when the load $R_L$ is high (S3, S5) and too low when the excitation $I_p$ is low (S4).
    *   This is a classic problem: we need a way to dump excess energy.
    *   Since we can't use a 5.5 V Zener, what if we use a "leaky" storage?
    *   Wait, `P-SSHI-Bleed` (c0042) tried a bleed resistor and failed miserably. Why?
        *   $R_{bleed} = 1\text{M}\Omega$.
        *   On S1, $R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$. Total load = $1\text{M} || 2.2\text{M} = 687\text{k}\Omega$.
        *   This is a much heavier load, which dragged $V_{out}$ down to 2.53 V.
        *   So a $1\text{M}\Omega$ bleed is too strong.

    *   What if we use a *very* high value bleed resistor? Or a non-linear bleed?
    *   A non-linear bleed could be a Zener diode. But the only Zener is 3.3 V.
    *   If we put a 3.3 V Zener in series with some diodes?
        *   DSCH $\approx 0.25$ V.
        *   $3.3 \text{ (Zener)} + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 \dots$
        *   To get to 5.5 V: $5.5 - 3.3 = 2.2$ V.
        *   $2.2 / 0.25 \approx 8-9$ diodes.
        *   That would use too many components.

    *   Let's try a different approach. Maybe we can improve the efficiency for S4.
    *   In `P-SSHI`, the inductor is used for inversion. The efficiency depends on $L$ and $t_{on}$.
    *   The `P-SSHI` design used $L=0.01$ H and $t_{on}=0.001$ s.
    *   Actually, $t_{on}$ for SSHI should be around $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   For $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50 \mu$s.
    *   The $t_{on}=0.001$ s (1 ms) used in `P-SSHI` is very long! This means the inductor is essentially a short circuit for a long time, possibly wasting energy or causing ringing.

    *   Let's try a more standard SSHI approach:
        1.  Smaller $t_{on}$ (around $50 \mu$s).
        2.  A larger output capacitor $C_{out}$ to reduce ripple and stabilize $V_{out}$.
        3.  A very large bleed resistor (e.g., $10\text{M}\Omega$) to prevent $V_{out}$ from skyrocketing on S3.

    *   Wait, I have another idea. Instead of a full bridge, what if I use a half-bridge with a capacitor?
    *   Actually, the full bridge is generally better for this.

    *   Let's try to refine the SSHI:
        *   L: 10 mH
        *   Cout: 1-10 $\mu$F
        *   $t_{on}$: $50 \mu$s
        *   S1: both edges
        *   Add a very large bleed resistor ($R_{bleed} = 10\text{M}\Omega$ or $20\text{M}\Omega$) to help with S3.

    *   Wait, let's look at the `P-SSHI` result for S4 again. $V_{avg} = 3.77$ V.
    *   To get it to 4.5 V, we need more efficiency.
    *   Is the current `P-SSHI` topology the best?
        *   Full bridge: 2 diode drops.
        *   What if we use a synchronous rectifier? We only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
